title: 08. Evaluation, Validation & Tuning: Model Evaluation Metrics
summary: Model evaluation metrics are quantitative measures used to assess the performance of machine learning models. Choosing the right metrics is crucial for understanding how well a model performs and for comparing different models.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Model evaluation metrics are quantitative measures used to assess the performance of machine learning models. Choosing the right metrics is crucial for understanding how well a model performs and for comparing different models. The choice of metrics depends on the type of problem (regression, classification, clustering) and the specific business context.

sections.title: Why Evaluation Metrics Matter
sections.body:
- **Model Selection**: Compare different algorithms and choose the best one
- **Hyperparameter Tuning**: Guide the optimization process
- **Business Impact**: Translate model performance to business value
- **Model Monitoring**: Track performance over time
- **Stakeholder Communication**: Explain results to non-technical audiences

sections.title: Regression Metrics
sections.body:
Regression metrics measure how well a model predicts continuous values. They focus on the difference between predicted and actual values.

### 1. Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
- **Formula**: MAE = (1/n) × Σ|y_true - y_pred|
- **Range**: [0, ∞)
- **Interpretation**: Average absolute difference between predictions and actual values
- **Advantages**: Easy to interpret, robust to outliers
- **Disadvantages**: Doesn't penalize large errors as heavily as MSE
- **When to use**: When you want to understand average error magnitude in the same units as the target

### 2. Mean Squared Error (MSE)
- **Formula**: MSE = (1/n) × Σ(y_true - y_pred)²
- **Range**: [0, ∞)
- **Interpretation**: Average squared difference between predictions and actual values
- **Advantages**: Penalizes large errors more heavily, differentiable
- **Disadvantages**: Sensitive to outliers, harder to interpret
- **When to use**: When large errors are particularly costly, for optimization algorithms

### 3. Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
- **Formula**: RMSE = √MSE
- **Range**: [0, ∞)
- **Interpretation**: Square root of MSE, in the same units as the target
- **Advantages**: Same units as target variable, penalizes large errors
- **Disadvantages**: Still sensitive to outliers
- **When to use**: When you want MSE benefits but need interpretable units

### 4. R-squared (Coefficient of Determination)
- **Formula**: R² = 1 - (SS_res / SS_tot) where SS_res = Σ(y_true - y_pred)², SS_tot = Σ(y_true - y_mean)²
- **Range**: (-∞, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Proportion of variance explained by the model
- **Advantages**: Scale-independent, intuitive interpretation
- **Disadvantages**: Can be misleading with non-linear relationships
- **When to use**: To understand how much variance the model explains

### 5. Adjusted R-squared
- **Formula**: Adjusted R² = 1 - [(1-R²)(n-1)/(n-p-1)] where n = samples, p = features
- **Range**: (-∞, 1]
- **Interpretation**: R-squared adjusted for number of features
- **Advantages**: Penalizes overfitting, better for model comparison
- **Disadvantages**: More complex interpretation
- **When to use**: When comparing models with different numbers of features

sections.title: Classification Metrics
sections.body:
Classification metrics measure how well a model predicts categorical labels. They focus on the accuracy of predictions and the balance between different types of errors.

### 1. Accuracy
- **Formula**: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
- **Range**: [0, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Proportion of correct predictions
- **Advantages**: Simple to understand and calculate
- **Disadvantages**: Misleading for imbalanced datasets
- **When to use**: Balanced datasets, when all errors are equally costly

### 2. Precision
- **Formula**: Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
- **Range**: [0, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Of predicted positives, how many were actually positive
- **Advantages**: Focuses on false positive errors
- **Disadvantages**: Doesn't consider false negatives
- **When to use**: When false positives are costly (e.g., spam detection)

### 3. Recall (Sensitivity)
- **Formula**: Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
- **Range**: [0, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Of actual positives, how many were correctly identified
- **Advantages**: Focuses on false negative errors
- **Disadvantages**: Doesn't consider false positives
- **When to use**: When false negatives are costly (e.g., disease detection)

### 4. F1 Score
- **Formula**: F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)
- **Range**: [0, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Harmonic mean of precision and recall
- **Advantages**: Balanced measure, considers both types of errors
- **Disadvantages**: May not be optimal for all use cases
- **When to use**: When you need a balanced measure of precision and recall

### 5. ROC-AUC Curve
- **Definition**: Plots True Positive Rate vs. False Positive Rate at various thresholds
- **Range**: [0, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Area under curve measures model's ability to distinguish classes
- **Advantages**: Threshold-independent, works well with imbalanced data
- **Disadvantages**: May not reflect performance at specific thresholds
- **When to use**: Overall model performance assessment, imbalanced datasets

### 6. Confusion Matrix
- **Definition**: Table showing TP, TN, FP, FN for each class
- **Interpretation**: Detailed breakdown of predictions vs. actual
- **Advantages**: Provides complete picture of model performance
- **Disadvantages**: Can be complex for multi-class problems
- **When to use**: Understanding specific types of errors, debugging models

### 7. Log Loss
- **Formula**: Log Loss = -Σ(y_true × log(y_pred) + (1-y_true) × log(1-y_pred))
- **Range**: [0, ∞)
- **Interpretation**: Penalizes confident wrong predictions heavily
- **Advantages**: Considers prediction confidence, differentiable
- **Disadvantages**: Sensitive to outliers, harder to interpret
- **When to use**: When you need probability estimates, optimization

sections.title: Clustering Metrics
sections.body:
Clustering metrics measure how well unsupervised learning algorithms group similar data points together.

### 1. Silhouette Score
- **Formula**: Silhouette = (b - a) / max(a, b) where a = average intra-cluster distance, b = average nearest-cluster distance
- **Range**: [-1, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Higher values indicate better clustering
- **Advantages**: Works without true labels, intuitive interpretation
- **Disadvantages**: Assumes convex clusters, computationally expensive
- **When to use**: When true labels are unknown, comparing clustering algorithms

### 2. Davies-Bouldin Index
- **Formula**: DB = (1/k) × Σ max(similarity between clusters)
- **Range**: [0, ∞)
- **Interpretation**: Lower values indicate better clustering
- **Advantages**: Works without true labels, considers cluster separation
- **Disadvantages**: Sensitive to cluster shapes
- **When to use**: Comparing different clustering algorithms

### 3. Calinski-Harabasz Index
- **Formula**: CH = [tr(Bk)/(k-1)] / [tr(Wk)/(n-k)] where Bk = between-cluster dispersion, Wk = within-cluster dispersion
- **Range**: [0, ∞)
- **Interpretation**: Higher values indicate better clustering
- **Advantages**: Works without true labels, considers both separation and cohesion
- **Disadvantages**: Assumes spherical clusters
- **When to use**: When clusters are expected to be well-separated

### 4. Inertia (for K-Means)
- **Formula**: Inertia = Σ(distance to cluster centroid)²
- **Range**: [0, ∞)
- **Interpretation**: Lower values indicate better clustering
- **Advantages**: Simple to calculate, directly related to K-Means objective
- **Disadvantages**: Only works for K-Means, doesn't consider cluster separation
- **When to use**: Comparing different k values in K-Means

sections.title: Advanced Metrics
sections.body:
### 1. Precision-Recall Curve
- **Definition**: Plots precision vs. recall at various thresholds
- **Use**: When dealing with imbalanced datasets
- **Advantages**: Better than ROC for imbalanced data
- **Disadvantages**: More complex to interpret

### 2. Cohen's Kappa
- **Formula**: κ = (po - pe) / (1 - pe) where po = observed accuracy, pe = expected accuracy
- **Range**: [-1, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Agreement beyond chance
- **Use**: When random guessing is a concern

### 3. Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)
- **Formula**: MCC = (TP×TN - FP×FN) / √[(TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)]
- **Range**: [-1, 1]
- **Interpretation**: Correlation between predicted and actual
- **Use**: Balanced measure for binary classification

### 4. Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)
- **Formula**: MAPE = (1/n) × Σ|(y_true - y_pred)/y_true| × 100
- **Range**: [0, ∞)
- **Interpretation**: Average percentage error
- **Use**: When relative errors are more important than absolute errors

sections.title: Metric Selection Guidelines
sections.body:
### For Regression Problems
1. **Start with**: RMSE and R-squared
2. **For outliers**: Consider MAE
3. **For relative errors**: Use MAPE
4. **For model comparison**: Use Adjusted R-squared

### For Classification Problems
1. **Balanced datasets**: Use Accuracy
2. **Imbalanced datasets**: Use Precision, Recall, F1-score
3. **Probability estimates**: Use Log Loss
4. **Overall assessment**: Use ROC-AUC
5. **Specific thresholds**: Use Precision-Recall curves

### For Clustering Problems
1. **K-Means**: Use Inertia and Silhouette Score
2. **General clustering**: Use Silhouette Score
3. **Algorithm comparison**: Use Davies-Bouldin Index
4. **Well-separated clusters**: Use Calinski-Harabasz Index

sections.title: Best Practices
sections.body:
### 1. Use Multiple Metrics
- No single metric captures all aspects of performance
- Combine different types of metrics for comprehensive evaluation
- Consider business context when choosing metrics

### 2. Consider Data Characteristics
- **Imbalanced data**: Use precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC
- **Outliers**: Use robust metrics like MAE
- **Scale**: Use scale-independent metrics when comparing across datasets

### 3. Cross-Validation
- Use cross-validation to get reliable estimates
- Report mean and standard deviation of metrics
- Consider the stability of metrics across folds

### 4. Business Context
- Align metrics with business objectives
- Consider costs of different types of errors
- Translate technical metrics to business impact

### 5. Model Comparison
- Use the same metrics for fair comparison
- Consider statistical significance
- Account for computational complexity

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
### 1. Over-relying on Accuracy
- **Problem**: Accuracy can be misleading for imbalanced datasets
- **Solution**: Use precision, recall, F1-score, or ROC-AUC

### 2. Ignoring Business Context
- **Problem**: Choosing metrics without considering business impact
- **Solution**: Align metrics with business objectives and costs

### 3. Not Using Cross-Validation
- **Problem**: Single train-test split may not be representative
- **Solution**: Use k-fold cross-validation for reliable estimates

### 4. Comparing Incompatible Metrics
- **Problem**: Comparing models using different metrics
- **Solution**: Use the same evaluation framework for all models

### 5. Ignoring Confidence Intervals
- **Problem**: Not accounting for uncertainty in metric estimates
- **Solution**: Report confidence intervals or standard deviations

sections.title: Tools and Libraries
sections.body:
### 1. Scikit-learn
- `sklearn.metrics`: Comprehensive collection of metrics
- `sklearn.model_selection`: Cross-validation utilities
- `sklearn.metrics.plot_*`: Visualization functions

### 2. Visualization Libraries
- **Matplotlib/Seaborn**: Basic metric plots
- **Plotly**: Interactive visualizations
- **Yellowbrick**: Specialized ML visualization

### 3. Specialized Libraries
- **Scikit-plot**: Additional plotting functions
- **MLxtend**: Extended metrics and utilities
